# Area

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

How large was the quantity at each date? `area` fills the
region between the data and a baseline at zero. Its top edge is the boundary a
`line` would draw, and the fill below that edge shows how large the quantity
was.

## Basic usage {#basic-usage}

How large were sales in each of five years? The `actuals` table holds the
sales of one year in each row, from 2019 to 2023. Most examples in this chapter
start from the smallest sentence that draws an area: the data, the mark, and its
two positions, `x` and `y`.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(actuals)
```

```{r}
data(actuals) + area + x(year) + y(sales) +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Sales, 2019 to 2023")
```

*"Given the actuals: an area, x is year, y is sales."*

Notice that the fill reaches the left and right edges of the panel. With `point`,
the axis ends a little past the data. A dot drawn at the last value would
otherwise be cut in half by the panel edge. An area has no dots. Its top
edge passes through the data values, so nothing can be cut off, and the axis ends exactly
at the first and last year. [Scales](../scales.qmd#the-axis-fits-your-data)
explains when an axis ends at the data and when it leaves a margin.

An area's two axes do different jobs. One is the **domain**, the axis the area
runs along, and the other is the **measure**, the quantity it fills up to. A
`line` has the same two axes. When one of a bar's two columns is a category,
swapping the columns on `x` and `y` turns the bar on its side. In the plot above
both columns are numbers, so the domain is `x`. A category is always the domain, on either
axis, so an area turns as a bar does. With the category on `y`, it is read down
the page and fills toward zero on `x`, as [A category on the
domain](#a-category-on-the-domain) shows. `density` reads a category
differently: its curve runs along the axis that does not hold the category, and
[With transforms](#with-transforms) shows both forms, the half violin and the
ridgeline plot.

## Why the fill starts at zero {#the-baseline-has-to-be-zero}

A `line` says *where* the value was; an `area` says *how much* there was. The
fill is the quantity, so it starts from zero. A fill that starts anywhere else
shows the height above that start, not the quantity itself. gog does not stop
you from starting the axis somewhere else. `y(sales, limits = c(100, NA))`
starts it at 100, and the `NA` leaves the top where the data puts it. The fill
starts at 100 too, and no warning is printed. That decision is yours to make:
the fill then shows sales minus 100 rather than the sales, and whoever reads
your plot has to know it.
[Scales](../scales.qmd#limits-stating-the-range-yourself) explains
`limits`.

So the choice of mark is about the data, not the appearance. Sales have a
**true zero**, where zero means none at all, so the first plot is correct: the
fill is the sales. Life expectancy in years has a true zero too, and several
plots below fill to it. A quantity whose zero is only a convention has no
amount for a fill to show. A temperature in degrees Celsius is one: 0 °C is
where water freezes, not the absence of heat. A calendar year is another: the
year 0 is not the absence of time. Draw those with `line`.

For life expectancy the data allows either mark, so the question you are asking
decides between them. An area and a line draw the same
top edge. Here is that edge drawn with `line` and split by `color`, as in the
[Line](line.qmd) chapter. It shows where each country's value was, and nothing
about how much:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_asia)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
  title("Life expectancy as lines, not quantities")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, color by country."*

## Multiple series {#multiple-series}

The table holds five countries, twelve years each, so the sentence has to
name the column that splits them. Without a split, the boundary runs through all
sixty rows as one region. `color` splits the rows into one **series** per
country, the rows that one region is drawn through, and names each country in a
legend. It is the same split that gives `line` one stroke per country. The
sentence also sets a low opacity, so the regions drawn first show through the
ones drawn over them:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(opacity = 0.45) +
  title("One region per country")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: areas, x is year, y is life, color by country."*

Five lines can cross without hiding each other, because a line is a thin
stroke. Five areas cannot: a fill covers whatever lies behind it, and at the
default opacity, 0.82, only a little shows through. Write the same sentence with no
opacity, and gog prints a warning before it draws:

```{r}
#| message: true
data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
  title("Five regions, no opacity set: each one covers the ones before it")
```

Compare the legend with the plot. Every country is named there, but five
regions cannot be distinguished. Each region covers the ones drawn before it,
so you can read a region only where it rises above every region drawn after
it. The warning is advice rather than a refusal: the sentence is legal, so gog
draws it.

The other way to draw it is to stack the regions instead of overlaying them.
That is written `area * stack`. `stack` is a collision modifier: it moves marks
that would otherwise be drawn in the same place, rather than summarizing them.
The other three move single marks: `dodge` sets them side by side within a
category's slot, the stretch of the axis that belongs to one category, `jitter` scatters them, and `repel` pushes labels apart. An
area is one connected shape across the axis, not a single mark, so it refuses
all three. With `stack`, each region starts at the top of the ones below it, so
the five form one stacked shape and none is covered:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + area * stack + x(year) + y(population) + color(country) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("Five Asian countries, population stacked")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: areas derived by stack, x is year, y is population,
color by country."*

Each country's region is as thick as its population, and the top edge of the
stack is the five-country total. This plot measures `population` instead of `life` on
purpose. You stack quantities that *add*: populations add up to a total that
means something, and life expectancies do not. gog does not stop you from
stacking them. Put `y(life)` in place of `y(population)` in the sentence above,
and gog draws five regions to a top edge that climbs from 229 in 1952 to
370 in 2007, with no warning. That
number means nothing. So use `stack` with care: you always get a plot, and only
you know whether the sum of the parts means something.

Which country's share of the five grew? The stacked plot cannot say, because
every region's baseline moves with the ones below it. `stack(share = TRUE)`
divides each country's value in a year by that year's total. The top edge of the
stack is then flat at 1, and each region's thickness is that country's share:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + area * stack(share = TRUE) + x(year) + y(population) +
  color(country) +
  y_label("Share of population") +
  title("Five Asian countries, population as shares")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: areas derived by stack as shares, x is year, y is
population, color by country."*

Between 1952 and 2007, India's share rose from 0.33 to 0.39, and Japan's fell
from 0.08 to 0.05. The total is gone from this plot: every year reaches 1, so it
shows which shares grew and no longer how large the total was. Draw both when
you need both answers. The
[Transforms](../transforms.qmd#stacked-areas-the-case-stack-was-built-for)
chapter covers `stack` in full, with a section on stacked areas.

Every stack so far was split by `color`. A stack can also be split by
[`group`](../channels.qmd#group). It splits the rows as `color` does, but every
region gets the same color and there is no legend. Use it when the total matters
more than telling the regions apart. Because the regions share one color, gog
draws a thin line between them in the panel's background color. A
stacked [bar](bar.qmd#splitting-without-color) separates its segments the same
way. The `channel_sales` table holds each quarter's `revenue` from two ways of
selling. Its `channel` column names them, Retail and Online:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(channel_sales)
```

```{r}
data(channel_sales) + area * stack + x(quarter) + y(revenue) + group(channel)
```

*"Given the channel sales table: areas derived by stack, x is quarter, y is
revenue, grouped by channel."*

`quarter` is a category, so each quarter gets a slot of its own, and the fill
runs from the middle of the first slot to the middle of the last.
[A category on the domain](#a-category-on-the-domain) describes this shape.

The top edge is each quarter's total. Retail comes first in the table, and gog
piles the series in that order, so Retail is the lower region. The thin line
marks where the retail region ends and the online region begins. No color or
legend tells the two regions apart. When the reader needs to know which is
which, split by `color` instead, which gives each region its own fill and a
legend entry. The thin line is not a border: an area takes
no border, as the next section explains. gog draws the line only when `group`
alone splits the stack, and no setting removes it.

## Giving an area an edge {#giving-an-area-an-edge}

A low opacity, like the 0.45 in [Multiple series](#multiple-series), leaves a
faint top edge, and the top edge is where the data is. A stroke along it makes
the boundary easy to read. An area takes no border of its own. To draw the
edge, layer a `line` over the area; the line traces the same top edge:

```{r}
data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  area + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.25) +
  line + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.5) +
  title("area + line: the fill and its edge, composed")
```

*"Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, an area and also a line."*

There is no border setting on `area` to use instead. A layered `line` gives the
edge its own color, width, opacity and dash. A bar's border settings,
`border_color` and `border_size`, give only a color and a width.

## One region, one fill {#one-region-one-fill}

The plot above set one opacity for the whole area. Can you map a column to an
area's opacity instead? No, and the reason is the shape. An area is a single
filled region, so `opacity` is a *setting* here and not a channel. Each row of
the table is one vertex, a corner of the top edge, not a piece of the fill.
No part of the region belongs to one row, so a column cannot make one row
lighter or darker than another. `opacity` is a setting on `line` for the same
reason.

`size` is refused both ways: `area` neither maps it nor sets it. A stroke has a
width, so `line` lets you set one. An area's extent comes from its x, its y and
its baseline, so there is no size to choose. Both marks take `style(color = )`
and `style(opacity = )`. [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows the refusals
for `opacity` and `size`.

## With transforms {#with-transforms}

Apart from the stack, every plot so far filled to values already in the table.
A transform computes new values first, and the area fills to what it computed.
A distribution, for example, can be drawn as a filled shape. The question is
the one a histogram answers: how many rows fall in each interval? `bin`,
`density` and the
[aggregation family](../transforms.qmd#aggregation-family-sum-mean-median-max-min-quantile)
mean the same thing on an area as on a bar. `bin` counts the rows in each
interval. The boundary then runs through the bin centers, and the region below
it is filled. That shape is the frequency polygon `line * bin` draws, with its
inside filled:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * bin + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("area * bin: a filled frequency polygon")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: an area derived by bin, x is life."*

`bin(30)` and `bin(width = 5)` set the bins here exactly as they do for a bar:
`bin(30)` cuts the axis into 30 intervals, and `bin(width = 5)` into intervals
five years wide.
[Choosing the bin count](../transforms.qmd#choosing-the-bin-count) shows both,
and [Choosing a width](../transforms.qmd#choosing-a-width) explains how to pick
a width.

`density` replaces the counts with a smooth curve, and the area fills the
region under it:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("area * density")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: an area derived by density, x is life."*

`density` is not the area's own transform. Other marks take it too, and only
the shape changes:

| Mark derived by `density` | Shape |
|---|---|
| `line * density` | the curve as a stroke |
| `step * density` | the curve as a staircase |
| `point * density` | one dot at each point where the curve was estimated |
| `bar * density` | one thin bar at each of those points |
| `ribbon * density` | with a category, the curve mirrored: the violin |
| `area * density` | the curve filled to the baseline, the plot above |

Put `line`, `step`, `point` or `bar` in place of `area` in the sentence above,
and each one draws. `ribbon` refuses it, because a ribbon spans between two
boundaries and one curve gives only one. With a category,
`ribbon * density + x(<category>) + y(<measure>)` draws the violin.

Give the `area * density` sentence a category on `x` and a number on `y`, and
the curve runs along `y` instead of `x`. Each continent gets its own estimate,
drawn inside its slot. The curve is one side of the violin that
`ribbon * density` draws, so this plot is called the **half violin**:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("area * density + x(continent): the half violin")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: areas derived by density, x is continent, y is life,
color by continent."*

The `area * density + x(life)` sentence above and this one differ in three
places: `x` moved from `life` to `continent`, `y(life)` was added, and so was
`color(continent)`. With only
`x(life)`, life runs along `x` and `y` holds no column, so `y` carries the
density estimate, as it carried the count for `bin`. With a category on `x` and
a number on `y`, both axes hold a column, so each estimate is drawn across its
category's slot, one distribution per continent. The slots already keep the
continents apart, so here `color` only paints: it gives each continent's region
its own fill and a legend entry, and without it the plot still draws one curve
per continent. On a `line` the same channel colors the stroke; on an area it
colors the fill.

Can the two columns trade axes? Yes, as they can for any area whose domain is a
category. Put life on `x` and the
category on `y`, and each curve runs along life, rising from its own
category's place on the `y` axis. That is the **ridgeline plot**, and it is the
half violin's sentence with `x` and `y` exchanged:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(life) + y(continent) +
  color(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: areas derived by density, x is life, y is continent,
color by continent."*

[Ribbon](ribbon.qmd#sideways-and-halved) shows all four forms in one section:
one side or two, and the category on either axis. Its
[violin section](ribbon.qmd#the-violin-a-distribution-per-category) says what
the width of a violin can mean.

The half violin and the ridgeline plot give each group a place of its own. To
compare the groups over the same stretch of the axis instead, overlay their
curves in one panel. Histograms of several groups drawn in one panel overlap:
the Bar chapter's [Overlaid histograms](bar.qmd#overlaid-histograms) section
draws three species of iris that way. Smooth curves are easier to distinguish,
because they cross at a point instead of sharing bin edges. The `iris_flowers`
table holds measurements of 150 iris flowers, 50 of each of three species.
`color(species)` splits the rows, so `density` makes one estimate for each
species, all in one panel.

As in [Multiple series](#multiple-series), a low opacity lets each region show
through the others. As in [Giving an area an edge](#giving-an-area-an-edge), a
`line` layered on top draws each region's top edge. The line takes `density`
too, so it traces the same curve the area fills. `color` is written before both
marks, so it reaches both layers, as [Encoding scope](../encoding-scope.qmd)
explains.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_flowers)
```

```{r}
data(iris_flowers) + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  area * density + style(opacity = 0.25) +
  line * density +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Petal length, one curve per species")
```

*"Given the iris flowers: x is petal length, color by species, areas derived by
density and also lines derived by density."*

The area under each density curve is 1, so the species whose petals vary least
draws the tallest curve. Every setosa petal is between 1.0 and 1.9 cm long, so
its curve is alone on the left and rises highest. Versicolor and virginica
petals overlap from 4.5 to 5.1 cm, and around there each fill shows through the
other. All three curves share one **bandwidth**, the width that decides how
smooth each curve is. So a difference in their shapes comes from the data, not
from the smoothing. [Transforms](../transforms.qmd#one-transform-four-readings)
explains how the shared bandwidth is chosen.

After `bin` and `density`, the third kind of transform is the aggregation
family: `sum`, `mean`, `median`, `max`, `min` and `quantile`. Each leaves one
value at each position on `x`, here one for each year, and the area fills to
those values, exactly as a bar would:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + area * mean + x(year) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("area * mean: five countries averaged per year")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: an area derived by mean, x is year, y is life."*

A transform can also add the values up along the axis.
[`cumulative`](../transforms.qmd#cumulative-the-running-total) adds each year's
value to the years before it, and the area fills to the total so far:

```{r}
data(actuals) + area * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
  title("area * cumulative: sales so far")
```

*"Given the actuals: an area derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales."*

The region rises from 120 in 2019 to 703 in 2023, the sales of all five years.
`stack` adds up the series at one year, and `cumulative` adds up the years of
one series. The two compose:
`area * cumulative * stack + x(week) + y(plays) + color(genre)`, over the
`listening` table's weekly plays of four music genres, piles each genre's plays
so far.

## A category on the domain {#a-category-on-the-domain}

The mean in the `area * mean` plot above was computed for each year, and year is
a continuous domain. Put a category there instead: over `gapminder_2007`,
`x(continent)` gives one mean per continent. One summary per category is
usually drawn as bars. An area draws the five continent means as one connected
shape instead. Use it when the reader should see one overall shape rather than
compare five heights. Each category gets one slot, and the boundary runs from
slot to slot in the order the continents first appear in the table: Asia,
Europe, Africa, the Americas, Oceania. The region still fills down to zero:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("area * mean + x(continent): the filled profile")
```

gog draws that sentence. The boundary runs from Asia to Oceania in axis order,
and the fill reaches from each mean down to zero. The segments between the
categories are where the plot can claim more than was measured. Nothing was
measured between Africa and the Americas, and a straight segment is drawn there
anyway. A line across that gap claims a change.
A fill claims a quantity as well, at every point between the two categories. If
you read only the vertices, the segments help you compare the five heights. If
you read the segments themselves, they claim what was never measured. To
compare the five means and nothing else, change `area` to `bar`: one word
changes, and there are no segments to read.

Keep the fill when the overall shape is what the reader should see. Continents
have no order, but a straight axis still puts one of them first and another
last. A circle has no first or last place. Add
[`polar()`](../polar.qmd#the-radar-a-categorical-angle), which places the
categories around a circle, and the same sentence
draws the filled **radar chart**:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * mean + x(continent) + y(life) + polar() +
    title("area * mean + polar(): the filled radar")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: an area derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, in
polar."*

The filled shape can also turn down the page, as [the line's
profile does](line.qmd#the-profile-turned). With the continents on `y` and the
means on `x`, the region fills toward zero on `x`, and Asia, the first continent
in the table, is at the top:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * mean + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("area * mean + y(continent): the filled profile, turned")
```

Africa, at 54.8 years, makes the deepest notch in the right edge, as it made the
lowest dip in the profile above. In `polar()` a turned area is refused, as a
[turned line](line.qmd#what-it-refuses) is.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms an area takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("area")
```

The plots below show every transform an area takes. Within a figure the plots
differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any
other change. [With transforms](#with-transforms) explains `bin`, `density`,
`mean` and `cumulative` in more detail.

**Counting.** `count` and `proportion` tally the rows at each value of `x`, on a
category or a number. `bin` and `density` work on a number. `bin` counts the
rows in each interval, and `density` estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely
the rows lie along the axis. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty,
and the area fills the region below it. The top two plots put `continent` on
`x`, so the boundary runs from slot to slot, as [A category on the
domain](#a-category-on-the-domain) describes. The bottom two put `life` on
`x`:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + area * count + x(continent) + title("area * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + area * proportion + x(continent) +
     title("area * proportion"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + area * bin + x(life) + title("area * bin")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(life) + title("area * density")))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: an area derived by count, x is continent, beside an area
derived by proportion, x is continent; above an area derived by bin, x is life,
beside an area derived by density, x is life."*

Look at the `y` axis of each plot. None of the four sentences writes `y()`,
yet each `y` axis has a name: Count, Proportion, Count and
Density. The table has no column by those names. Each transform writes one, and
`y` draws it. `count` and `bin` write `count`, the number of rows at each value
or in each interval. `proportion` writes `proportion`, each count's share of all
the rows. `density` writes `density`, the height of the estimated curve. The
axis is labeled with the column's name, capitalized, as [The name on a measure
axis](../transforms.qmd#the-name-on-a-measure-axis) explains.

**Summaries.** The six summaries reduce the rows at each value of `x` to one
value, so they need a number on `y`. The `gapminder_asia` table holds five
countries in each year, so each summary turns five values into one. `sum` reads
`population`, because only an amount has a total that means something. The
other five read `life`. They give the mean, the median, the largest and the
smallest value, and `quantile(0.9)` gives the value that nine tenths of the rows
fall below:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_asia) + area * sum + x(year) + y(population) +
    title("area * sum")) |
  (data(gapminder_asia) + area * mean + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("area * mean")) |
  (data(gapminder_asia) + area * median + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("area * median"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_asia) + area * max + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("area * max")) |
     (data(gapminder_asia) + area * min + x(year) + y(life) +
        title("area * min")) |
     (data(gapminder_asia) + area * quantile(0.9) + x(year) + y(life) +
        title("area * quantile(0.9)")))
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: an area derived by sum, x is year, y is population,
beside an area derived by mean, x is year, y is life, beside an area derived by
median, x is year, y is life; above an area derived by max, x is year, y is
life, beside an area derived by min, x is year, y is life, beside an area
derived by quantile at 0.9, x is year, y is life."*

The five plots that read `life` share one scale, so their heights can be
compared from plot to plot.

**Fitted lines.** `smooth` and `straight` need a number on each axis. They fit a
line to the rows, each placed at its `x` and its `y`. `smooth` follows the shape
of the data, and `straight` is the least-squares line. A fitted line is usually
drawn with `line`, as a curve or a straight line over the points ([Smoothed
trend line](line.qmd#smoothed-trend-line)). The area fills the region below each
fitted line, down to zero.

**Running total.** `cumulative` adds each value to the ones before it along the
axis. The third plot reads the `actuals` table, shown in [Basic
usage](#basic-usage), with `year` on `x` and `sales` on `y`:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + area * smooth + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   title("area * smooth")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + area * straight + x(gdp) + y(life) +
     title("area * straight")) |
  (data(actuals) + area * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
     title("area * cumulative"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: an area derived by smooth, x is gdp, y is life, beside
an area derived by straight, x is gdp, y is life; beside an area from the
actuals, derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales."*

**Collision modifiers.** Collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on
top of one another. `stack` is the only one
an area takes. It piles the regions of a split on top of each other, so it needs
`color`, `pattern` or `group` to make more than one region. `stack(share = TRUE)` divides
each region's height by the total at the same `x`, so the top edge is flat at 1.
Stack an amount that adds up, such as `population`, as [Multiple
series](#multiple-series) explains:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_asia) + area * stack + x(year) + y(population) +
    color(country) + title("area * stack")) /
   (data(gapminder_asia) + area * stack(share = TRUE) + x(year) +
      y(population) + color(country) + title("area * stack(share = TRUE)"))) +
  theme(height = 800)
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: areas derived by stack, x is year, y is population,
color by country, above areas derived by stack as shares, x is year, y is
population, color by country."*

An area refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. The pair transforms
give `y` a low and a high at each value of `x`, and [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) fills
the band between them. `dodge` and `jitter` move each bar or point within a
category's slot, and an area is one connected shape across the axis.
[`point`](point.qmd) takes both. [`bar`](bar.qmd), [`interval`](interval.qmd),
[`box`](box.qmd) and [`text`](text.qmd) take `dodge`. `repel` moves [`text`](text.qmd)
labels off each other. `partition`, `flow` and `cluster` lay out rectangles,
bands and branches, which [`zone`](zone.qmd), [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) and [`path`](path.qmd)
draw. `layout` places a network, which [`point`](point.qmd), [`text`](text.qmd) and [`edge`](edge.qmd)
draw.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A setting changes how the region looks without reading a column, and each mark
takes its own. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are an area's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("area")
```

That is the shortest settings list in the book, shared with `ribbon`. `line`
has one more, `size`, and `bar` has three more: `border_color`, `border_size`
and `gap`. Each is left out on purpose: [One region, one
fill](#one-region-one-fill) explains `size`, [Giving an area an
edge](#giving-an-area-an-edge) explains the border, and `gap` is a share of the
slot a bar fills, and an area does not fill a slot. The one setting this chapter
has not shown yet is `pattern`, a
texture on the fill. The plot below hatches the fill and draws the edge with a
layered `line`, as before:

```{r}
data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  area + style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "hatch", opacity = 0.5) +
  line + style(color = "seagreen", size = 2) +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A textured fill, and a line for the edge")
```

*"Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, an area colored seagreen, with
pattern hatch and opacity 0.5, and also a line colored seagreen, with size 2."*

That layered line traces only the top boundary. A border would also draw a line
along the two sides and the baseline.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

gog refuses five kinds of area sentence: a category on both axes, `bin` on a
category, a mapped `opacity`, any `size`, and a split that leaves one position
in every series. The first two come from an axis. The first comes from the
measure. A region fills to a baseline at zero, and a category has no zero, so
one axis must hold a continuous column. With categories on both axes there is
nothing to
fill:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + area + x(continent) + y(country)
```

A category on one axis alone is accepted, on either axis. On `y`, beside a
number on `x`, the area turns down the page ([A category on the domain](#a-category-on-the-domain)),
and with `density` it is the ridgeline plot in [With
transforms](#with-transforms).

The second comes from the domain. `bin` cuts a continuous axis into intervals,
and a category is one slot with no width to cut. The message names `count`, the
transform that tallies the rows in each category:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + area * bin + x(continent)
```

`density` needs a continuous axis too. Alone, its column goes on `x`; with a
categorical column on one axis, the continuous column goes on the other, `x`
or `y`. A categorical column with no continuous column beside it is refused, and
the message names `bar * proportion` for the share of rows in each category:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(continent)
```

The next two come from the region's shape. A mapped `opacity` is the third. Each row is
one vertex of the top edge, so no part of the region belongs to a single row,
as [One region, one fill](#one-region-one-fill) explained.

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(year) + y(life) + opacity(gdp)
```

A `size` is the fourth, and it is refused both ways. An area's extent comes
from its x, its y and its baseline, so there is no size to map and none to
set:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(actuals) + area + x(year) + y(sales) + style(size = 4)
```

A `line` takes `style(size = )`, because a stroke has a width to set.

The fifth comes from the series. An area needs at least two positions in
each series, as a line does. Split by `color(continent)`, each continent's
series holds one mean, so the plot would draw nothing, and gog refuses it:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + area * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + style(opacity = 0.5)
```

[Line](line.qmd#what-it-refuses) shows the same refusal for `line`.

## In short {#in-short}

An area reads a category as its domain, on either axis, as a bar does, so a
category on `y` turns it down the page. With two numbers its domain is `x`.
`density` reads a category on either axis as the slot its curve is drawn in. An area's interior belongs to no single row, so `opacity` can only
be set. Its extent comes from its x, its y and its baseline, so `size` is
refused both ways.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

An area's top edge runs straight from one value to the next, so it shows the
value changing steadily in between. [Step](step.qmd) shows instead that each
value held until the next one, and then jumped.
